items.title: L12: Specifying clearance when a post changes
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls; National Security Vetting guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Posts change. A team picks up a new piece of work, a project starts handling more sensitive material, or a role is restructured. As a manager you are usually the person who notices that the access a post needs has moved, and who must raise it with the security or vetting team through the department's process. The starting point is to describe the access, not the person: what classification of material the holder will see, how often, whether the access is regular or occasional, whether they will work unescorted in sensitive sites, and whether any special handling or caveats apply. The vetting level is then chosen by security specialists to fit that description. Several practical points follow. A change of post can mean a change of clearance level, so you should not assume the previous clearance covers the new role. Clearance is usually granted for a defined purpose and level, and may need to be reviewed or renewed after a period set by the department. You must not give access ahead of clearance simply because the work is urgent; where interim access is allowed at all, it is a decision for security and is normally limited and supervised. It is also good practice to avoid building roles so that everybody needs high clearance when much of the work could be done by a small cleared group with others working on less sensitive material. That keeps the cleared pool manageable, keeps recruitment open to more people and reduces the intrusion on private lives. Finally, recheck periodically whether clearance held by your team still matches the work they do, and remove access that is no longer needed.

questions.prompt: A project your team runs begins to handle more sensitive material. What should the manager do first?

options.text: Describe the new access needed and raise it with security through the department's process
Ask each team member to apply for the highest clearance in case it is needed later
Ask each team member to apply for the highest clearance now, in case it is needed later on
Move the sensitive material to a shared folder so that the whole team can still see it

questions.hint: Start from the access the post needs and let specialists set the level.

questions.prompt: When describing the access a post needs, which detail is most useful to security?

options.text: The grade of the post holder and the length of time they have worked for the department
The names of the colleagues who currently hold the same level of clearance
The classification of material, how often it will be seen and whether access is regular or occasional
The manager's own view on whether the person can be trusted with sensitive work

questions.hint: Security needs the nature of the access, not opinions about the person.

questions.prompt: An EO is moving to a post with a different level of access. Which assumption is unsafe?

options.text: That the new post may need a different clearance level from the old one
That the clearance held for the previous role automatically covers the new one
That security should be told about the move before access is arranged
That the old access should be reviewed and removed if it is no longer needed in the new role

questions.hint: A change of post can mean a change of clearance.

questions.prompt: The team is under pressure and a cleared colleague is off sick. A manager proposes letting an uncleared person take over the sensitive work. What is the correct position?

options.text: It is acceptable if the uncleared person signs a note promising to keep the material confidential
It is acceptable if the manager supervises the person for the whole period of the cover
It is acceptable so long as the material is at SECRET rather than TOP SECRET
Urgency does not justify access ahead of clearance; any interim arrangement is a decision for security

questions.hint: Interim access, where allowed at all, is for security to approve.

questions.prompt: Why is it good practice not to give every role in a team the highest clearance?

options.text: It keeps recruitment open, reduces intrusion into private lives and keeps the cleared pool manageable
Higher levels of clearance expire sooner when they are held by large groups of people
It stops the vetting authority from carrying out any checks on the other staff in the team
It would breach the Official Secrets Act for too many people to hold clearance

questions.hint: Proportionality benefits both candidates and the organisation.

questions.prompt: How might a manager reduce the number of roles that need high clearance?

options.text: Reclassify the material at a lower level so that fewer people need to be cleared to see it
Ask staff to share their security passes so that cover is always available
Remove the need to check clearance by making every post a probationary post
Structure the work so a small cleared group handles the sensitive material and others handle the rest

questions.hint: Work design can limit the need for clearance without weakening security.

questions.prompt: A clearance is granted for a particular level and purpose. What follows from this?

options.text: It lasts for life once granted, whichever posts the person later holds
It may need to be reviewed or renewed under the department's rules, and it does not travel automatically to other posts
It lapses automatically each time the person is promoted
It can be used for any purpose so long as the person remains in the same department

questions.hint: Clearance is tied to a level and purpose and is not permanent.

questions.prompt: Who sets the vetting level for a post once the access has been described?

options.text: The line manager, once they have chosen whichever level of clearance seems appropriate
The candidate, who states the level of clearance they would be prepared to be vetted at
Security specialists, using the description of the access the post will have
The recruitment panel, as part of the final scoring and discussion at the interview

questions.hint: Managers describe the access; specialists decide the level.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager periodically recheck whether the clearances held in the team still match the work?

options.text: Departments are obliged to renew every clearance every year without exception
Clearances that are not rechecked automatically become Developed Vetting
The vetting authority withdraws clearance from teams that have not been rechecked
Work changes over time, and access that is no longer needed should be removed

questions.hint: Matching access to current need is a continuing duty.

questions.prompt: Which of these is least consistent with the principle that clearance follows access need?

options.text: Asking whether the post will see SECRET material regularly
Requiring SC for a post because the previous holder happened to have it
Asking whether the post needs unescorted access to a sensitive site
Asking whether a caveat or special handling rule applies to the material the work will involve

questions.hint: Copying the previous holder's clearance is habit, not analysis.

items.title: L12: Aftercare and changes of circumstances
items.source: National Security Vetting guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls, GOV.UK
items.body: Getting clearance is not the end of the process. Vetting is followed by aftercare, which means the continuing management of the security of cleared people. Aftercare is shared between the individual, their line manager and the department's security team. Cleared staff are expected to tell security about relevant changes in their circumstances. Examples usually include a change of relationship status, a new close relationship, significant financial difficulty, changes to residence or long stays abroad, new contacts with foreign nationals that go beyond ordinary social contact, a criminal charge or conviction, and a change in health that could affect reliability. This is not intended to punish people for having ordinary lives. The aim is for the department to know about circumstances that could make someone more vulnerable to pressure or to poor judgement, and to offer support early. Security staff, not the line manager, assess the significance of a change. A manager's role is to make sure staff know the duty, to listen and signpost without prying, to keep what they learn confidential on a need-to-know basis, and to pass on any concern about a person's reliability to the right place. Managers should also support people who are going through difficulties, because stress, debt and isolation can all increase risk. Many departments have an annual security appraisal or review for cleared staff, which asks the manager to confirm they have no concerns and gives an opportunity to raise any. Honest reporting, made promptly, usually counts in a person's favour. Concealment, on the other hand, can be the serious issue.

questions.prompt: What does aftercare mean in national security vetting?

options.text: A second round of vetting questions asked in the first week of a new job
A welfare service offered only to staff who leave the department
The continuing management of the security of cleared people after clearance is granted
A payment made to staff who have been cleared at higher levels

questions.hint: Aftercare continues after clearance is granted.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for aftercare?

options.text: The individual, their line manager and the department's security team share it
The vetting authority alone, once it has granted the clearance
The individual alone, as their own personal responsibility
The HR team alone, through the annual appraisal cycle

questions.hint: It is a shared responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which of these changes would cleared staff usually be expected to report?

options.text: A change of lunch routine or a new commuting route
A decision to take up a new hobby at weekends
A significant financial difficulty or a new close relationship
A change of mobile phone provider

questions.hint: Reportable changes are those that could affect vulnerability or reliability.

questions.prompt: Why does aftercare ask staff to report changes of circumstance?

options.text: To let the department spot vulnerability to pressure early and offer support
To build up a record that can be used if disciplinary action is needed later
To confirm that staff are following the rules about outside interests
To give managers background about the private lives of their teams

questions.hint: The purpose is early awareness and support.

questions.prompt: A cleared team member tells you they are in serious debt. What is the right response?

options.text: Tell the person that their clearance will be removed and they should look for another job
Share the details with the team so that colleagues can offer help
Decide yourself whether the debt matters and record it in your own notes only
Listen, signpost to the reporting route and support services, and keep it confidential on a need-to-know basis

questions.hint: Managers support and signpost; security assesses.

questions.prompt: Who assesses how significant a reported change is for someone's clearance?

options.text: The line manager, because they know the person best
Security staff, not the line manager
The person's closest colleague in the team
The HR business partner, using the contract

questions.hint: Security staff make that judgement.

questions.prompt: A manager notices that a cleared colleague seems increasingly isolated and anxious. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Ignore it because the colleague's personal life is none of the manager's business
Quietly reduce the colleague's access without telling anyone
Offer support, point to wellbeing services and, if there is a reliability concern, pass it to the right place
Raise it with the whole team so that people understand why the person may be behaving differently

questions.hint: Support first; raise concerns through the proper route.

questions.prompt: How is honest and prompt reporting of a change usually viewed?

options.text: As an admission that the person is no longer trustworthy to hold their current clearance
As a reason for the clearance to be withdrawn automatically, without any review
As neutral, since reporting changes is optional for cleared staff and carries no weight
As a point in the person's favour, because it shows reliability

questions.hint: Concealment is the bigger problem.

questions.prompt: What is the typical purpose of an annual security review of cleared staff?

options.text: To rank cleared staff against each other for promotion
To confirm managers have no concerns and to give a chance to raise any
To refresh the vetting questionnaire in full every year
To award a security bonus to staff with no incidents

questions.hint: It is a check-in, not a ranking or full re-vet.

questions.prompt: Which of these would be an inappropriate manager response when someone reports a change in circumstances?

options.text: Questioning the person in detail about their private life beyond what security has asked
Explaining where to report the change
Keeping the information confidential on a need-to-know basis
Making clear that the report was welcome

questions.hint: Managers should not pry.

items.title: L12: Running a security-conscious team day to day
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; Government Functional Standard for Security, GOV.UK
items.body: Policy is only useful if it works in the ordinary routines of a team. Several everyday areas deserve attention from a manager. Visitors should be signed in, wear passes and be escorted unless cleared for unescorted access. Staff should challenge, politely, anyone without a pass in a secure area, and should not hold doors open for people they do not know, which is called tailgating. Clear desk and clear screen habits matter because papers and screens can be read by cleaners, visitors or contractors. When working remotely, people should use approved devices and networks, avoid being overlooked in public places, take care with calls in earshot of others and keep devices and papers secure, including at home. The guidance on classifications sets out the marking OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET, with OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE used as a handling caveat for particularly sensitive OFFICIAL material. Most government work is OFFICIAL, and the basic principle for all levels is need to know: access should be limited to those who need the information to do their job. Aggregated information may deserve higher protection than its separate parts. Meetings can raise problems: sensitive topics should not be discussed in cafes, trains or lifts, and people should check who is in the room or on a call. Personal devices and personal email should not be used for official work unless the department's policy allows. A manager sets the tone by following the rules visibly, explaining the reasons, making it easy to comply by providing approved tools, and reacting calmly to mistakes. Security that is seen as an obstacle tends to be bypassed, so rules should be proportionate and explained.

questions.prompt: A visitor without a pass is walking alone through a secure area. What should a member of staff do?

options.text: Assume the visitor is lost and leave them to find their own way
Ignore them, as it is not the member of staff's job to police the building
Politely challenge them and, if needed, escort them or call security
Ask them to follow quietly behind and avoid attracting attention

questions.hint: Staff are expected to challenge unfamiliar people in secure areas.

questions.prompt: What does tailgating mean in a building security context?

options.text: Delaying the reporting of an incident until a convenient moment, so as not to cause alarm
Copying a document without permission and passing it to someone outside the team
Sending the same email to several people in a department at once for efficiency
Following someone through a secure door without using your own pass

questions.hint: Tailgating bypasses access control.

questions.prompt: Why do clear desk and clear screen habits matter?

options.text: They are needed only for TOP SECRET material
Papers and screens can be read by cleaners, visitors and contractors
They help the department to reduce its printing costs
They are required only when senior leaders are visiting

questions.hint: Anyone passing may see what is left out.

questions.prompt: A team member plans to take a sensitive call on a crowded train. What should the manager advise?

options.text: Avoid the call or discuss only what can safely be heard by anyone
Take the call but speak quietly so that others cannot hear
Take the call if they use headphones and a privacy screen
Take the call and write up the discussion later, so that it is recorded

questions.hint: Public places are unsuitable for sensitive discussions.

questions.prompt: Which principle applies at every classification level?

options.text: First come, first served
Need to know
Seniority of the person asking
Majority decision of the team

questions.hint: Access is limited to those who need it for their job.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE caveat?

options.text: A fourth classification, above TOP SECRET, reserved for information about foreign states
A label showing that the information is publicly available and may safely be shared
A marking used only on emails that are sent outside the department to other bodies
A handling caveat for particularly sensitive OFFICIAL material

questions.hint: It sits within OFFICIAL as a handling instruction.

questions.prompt: Why might a collection of individually low-risk documents deserve higher protection?

options.text: Combined documents are always legally privileged, however low each one is on its own
Departments must reclassify any folder with more than ten documents
Together they may reveal more than any single document, a point known as aggregation
The documents become subject to the National Security Act once stored together

questions.hint: Aggregation can raise the impact of loss.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to make security easier for the team to follow. Which approach fits the guidance?

options.text: Provide approved tools and explain the reasons behind the rules
Add more rules so that fewer decisions are left to individuals
Remove rules that staff find inconvenient, to keep goodwill
Rely on annual reminders and leave staff to find their own way in between

questions.hint: Rules that are proportionate and easy are followed.

questions.prompt: Why is security that is seen as an obstacle likely to fail?

options.text: Staff are legally entitled to ignore any rule that slows them down
Rules cannot be enforced unless the manager has Developed Vetting
People tend to bypass rules that seem pointless or hard to follow
Obstructive rules automatically lapse after a period of non-use

questions.hint: Behaviour follows perceived sense and ease.

questions.prompt: Which is the general position on using personal email for official work?

options.text: It is acceptable for anything that is classified at OFFICIAL and no higher
It is acceptable provided the person's manager is copied in to every message
It is acceptable whenever the official system is slow or unavailable for a time
It should not be used unless the department's policy allows it

questions.hint: Departmental policy governs, and the default is no.

items.title: L12: Incident triage in practice
items.source: Government Functional Standard for Security; departmental incident guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: When something goes wrong, a manager has to take quick decisions with incomplete information. A useful approach is to act in a sensible order. First, make people safe if there is any risk to them. Second, stop the harm spreading where that can be done safely: lock or disable accounts through the proper team, retrieve or recall a message, secure a door or area. Third, report to security and to anyone else the policy names, quickly and with the facts you have. Fourth, preserve evidence: keep the suspicious email, note times, avoid wiping devices until told. Fifth, support the person involved and avoid blame while the facts emerge. Sixth, help the specialists to assess what happened and what should change. Judging severity depends on what was exposed, to whom and for how long. A misdirected email with sensitive information to a trusted colleague in the same department is less serious than one sent to a member of the public or to an external organisation. A lost laptop that is fully encrypted and quickly reported is less serious than an unencrypted one, but still needs reporting. Do not let the apparent lack of harm stop you reporting; the person who has the facts to judge the harm is usually security, not you. Avoid speculating in writing about who is to blame. Where a pattern appears, such as several similar near misses in a team, raise it, because systems that allow repeated errors may be the problem. A calm, structured response often matters as much as the technical fix.

questions.prompt: Which is the best order of actions when an incident is discovered?

options.text: Make people safe, stop harm spreading, report, preserve evidence, then support those involved
Find who is to blame, tell the team, report to security and then fix the problem
Wait to see how serious it is, fix it quietly and report only if it grows
Delete anything that looks suspicious, report it and then investigate alone

questions.hint: Safety, containment, reporting and evidence come first.

questions.prompt: Which factor most affects how serious a misdirected email is?

options.text: The grade of the person who sent it, since senior staff are held to a higher standard
What was exposed, to whom and for how long
The time of day at which it was sent, since evening emails are less often read
The length of the email, since short messages are less likely to contain personal data

questions.hint: Severity depends on content, recipient and duration.

questions.prompt: Compare two incidents: an unencrypted laptop lost with personal data on it, and an encrypted laptop lost with the same data. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Report only the unencrypted one, since encryption means there is no incident
Report neither, as laptops can easily be replaced
Report both, but the unencrypted one is likely to be treated as more serious
Treat both identically, since encryption has no bearing on risk

questions.hint: Encryption can reduce, not remove, the need to report.

questions.prompt: A manager thinks an incident caused no harm. What should they do?

options.text: Record it in a team log and review it at the next regular team meeting
Report it anyway, because security is better placed to judge harm
Keep it quiet to avoid worrying the team unnecessarily
Wait until an external complaint arrives before taking any action about it

questions.hint: Reporting does not depend on the manager's view of harm.

questions.prompt: Why preserve the original suspicious email rather than delete it at once?

options.text: Deleting emails is a disciplinary offence in every case
The email will automatically alert other staff if left in the inbox
The ICO requires a copy of every suspicious email within a day
It may be needed as evidence to understand and contain the attack

questions.hint: Evidence helps specialists assess and contain.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager avoid writing speculation about blame in an incident report?

options.text: Facts are needed first, and speculation can be unfair and unhelpful
Reports must be written by the person who made the mistake, not by the manager
Blame is determined solely by the ICO after it has reviewed the report in full
Incident reports are published on the department's website so that the public can see them

questions.hint: Stick to facts; judgements follow investigation.

questions.prompt: Three near misses with misaddressed emails happen in a team over a month. What does good practice suggest?

options.text: Raise the pattern and look at whether a process or system change would prevent them
Treat each one separately and ignore any link between them
Warn the team to be more careful and take no further action
Disable email for the team until the cause has been found

questions.hint: Repeated near misses may point to a system problem.

questions.prompt: A door to a secure area is found propped open and nobody is around. What is the right immediate action?

options.text: Leave it as it is and mention it at the next team meeting if it is still open
Wait to see whether anyone returns before deciding whether to say anything about it
Photograph the open door and post the image to the team chat for everyone to see
Close it or secure the area if safe to do so and tell security

questions.hint: Secure the area and report promptly.

questions.prompt: What matters about the response to an incident beyond the technical fix?

options.text: A rapid public statement that explains what went wrong
A review of every other team's security arrangements
A calm, structured response that supports staff and encourages future reporting
An immediate change of team leader

questions.hint: Tone shapes whether people report next time.

questions.prompt: A colleague is distressed after clicking a malicious link. What should the manager do alongside reporting?

options.text: Ask them to resign from the project until the investigation ends
Reassure them, avoid blame and make sure they know what has been done
Tell them to say nothing to anyone until the investigation is complete
Remove their access to all systems for a month as a precaution

questions.hint: Support helps maintain a reporting culture.

items.title: L12: Personal data breaches: scenarios
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; UK GDPR, GOV.UK
items.body: Applying the breach rules is easier with a few practical habits. First, ask what personal data is involved and about how many people. Names and work email addresses are personal data. Special category data, such as health, ethnicity, religion or trade union membership, and data relating to criminal convictions, carries higher risk if exposed. Second, ask who has it now. A recipient inside the same team who is bound by confidentiality is a lower risk than a member of the public or an unknown external address. Third, ask whether it can be recovered or contained. A recalled message, a confirmed deletion, or a device wiped remotely can reduce the likelihood of harm. Fourth, tell the specialists straight away. They will decide whether it is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms and whether the ICO must be notified within 72 hours of the department becoming aware. They will also decide whether the people affected should be told, which is required when there is a likely high risk. A breach is not just a cyber attack. Common causes include emails sent to the wrong person, using the copy field instead of the blind copy field for a group mailing, leaving papers on public transport, attaching the wrong file, sharing a folder with too wide an audience, and unauthorised access by staff who are curious about a record. Looking at personal data without a work reason can itself be a breach and may be a criminal offence. After a breach, record what happened, what was done, and what has been changed to reduce the chance of repeat.

questions.prompt: A mass email to service users shows all recipients' addresses in the copy field instead of the blind copy field. How should this be viewed?

options.text: As a formatting error that does not need reporting if nobody complains
As a personal data breach, to be reported internally straight away
As a matter for the recipients to raise if they object
As a breach only if the addresses are personal ones rather than work ones

questions.hint: Disclosing addresses to others is a breach even if accidental.

questions.prompt: Why is special category data treated as higher risk if exposed?

options.text: Because it is always classified at SECRET
Because it can be disclosed only by the ICO
Because it cannot be corrected once recorded
Because its exposure can cause serious harm, for example discrimination or distress

questions.hint: Sensitive categories carry greater potential harm.

questions.prompt: Which recipient makes a misdirected email least concerning?

options.text: A colleague in the same team who is bound by confidentiality
A member of the public with a similar name
An unknown external address
A journalist who has made previous enquiries

questions.hint: Who has the data matters.

questions.prompt: A staff member looks at a family friend's record on the system out of curiosity. How is this treated?

options.text: As acceptable, since the person already has authorised access to the whole system
As a breach only if the friend later discovers it and complains to the department
As unauthorised access that can be a breach and may be a criminal offence
As an issue only for the line manager to deal with informally

questions.hint: Access needs a work reason.

questions.prompt: Which step reduces the likelihood of harm after a misdirected email, where practicable?

options.text: Asking the recipient to delete it and confirm that they have done so
Waiting to see whether the recipient reports it before deciding whether to tell anybody
Sending the same email again, with the sender's manager copied in so that it is checked
Deleting the sent email from the sender's own account only

questions.hint: Containment limits further spread.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether the ICO must be notified?

options.text: The person who made the mistake, as part of their own self-report to the team
The line manager, once the whole team has discussed it and reached a view
The department's specialists, using the facts the manager provides
The affected individuals, by agreeing among themselves whether the ICO should be told

questions.hint: Specialists make the call.

questions.prompt: When must affected people be told directly?

options.text: Whenever any personal data is involved, whatever the risk to the people concerned
When the breach is likely to result in a high risk to them
Only when the ICO instructs the department to do so
Only when someone has complained about the breach

questions.hint: High risk triggers direct notice.

questions.prompt: A manager is told on Friday afternoon of a breach discovered on Thursday. Why does speed still matter?

options.text: The ICO's offices are closed at weekends and so cannot be told
The breach must be fixed before the next working week begins
Breaches become more serious with every passing hour regardless of the facts
The 72-hour period runs from when the organisation became aware, so time is already running

questions.hint: Awareness starts the clock.

questions.prompt: What should be recorded after a breach?

options.text: What happened, what was done and what has been changed to reduce repeat
Only the name of the person who caused it
Only the number of people affected
Only the outcome if the ICO was told

questions.hint: Records support learning and accountability.

questions.prompt: Which cause counts as a personal data breach?

options.text: Saving a document to the proper folder, which only the right team members can access
Attaching the wrong spreadsheet to an email sent outside the department
Saving a document in the proper folder
Printing a document and storing it in a locked cabinet in the team's secure area

questions.hint: Wrong attachment can disclose data to those not entitled.

items.title: L12: Conflicts in recruitment and procurement
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Government Commercial Function guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Recruitment and procurement are two areas where conflicts of interest regularly arise, because decisions affect people's livelihoods and public money. In recruitment, the Recruitment Principles require appointment on merit after fair and open competition. A panel member who has a close personal relationship with a candidate, a financial link, or a history that could influence them should declare it before the process starts. In most cases they will be replaced, although a minor, remote link may be managed by the panel chair noting it. Candidates who are known to you through work are not automatically a problem, but a close friendship or family tie is. A manager must not give a candidate coaching or inside information not available to others. In procurement, officials evaluating bids must be able to show that the process was impartial and transparent. Conflicts can arise from a past employer, a shareholding, a family business, a close friendship with a bidder, or an expectation of future employment with a supplier. Declarations should be collected from everyone involved before bids are opened and refreshed if circumstances change. A conflict does not always require a person to leave, but the safest course is for them to step back from scoring or decisions on the affected bid, and from sharing information with others. Keep a record of the declaration and the decision on how to handle it. The point is as much to protect those involved from later challenge as to prevent bias. If someone is found to have taken part while conflicted and undeclared, the process may be challenged or the contract awarded may be reviewed.

questions.prompt: A panel member realises, on the morning of the interviews, that one candidate is a close friend. When should the link be declared?

options.text: After the candidate has been scored, so that the effect on the result can be judged
Only if the candidate reaches the shortlist for a second round
Only if another panel member or the candidate raises it first
Straight away, before any interview begins, so the panel can be adjusted

questions.hint: Declare early so that the process is protected.

questions.prompt: A panel member has declared a close friendship with a candidate. Which response is the safest?

options.text: Ask the panel member to score that candidate last, to limit any influence
Ask the candidate to withdraw, since the competition cannot proceed otherwise
Replace the panel member for that recruitment and record why
Keep the link between the two of them from the other panel members

questions.hint: Replacement is the usual safe course.

questions.prompt: Which action would breach fairness in a recruitment exercise?

options.text: Giving every candidate the same published job pack and criteria
Offering reasonable adjustments to candidates who need them for the process
Scoring each candidate against the same published criteria
Coaching one candidate on likely questions that the others will not see

questions.hint: Inside help undermines fair and open competition.

questions.prompt: Why should conflict declarations in a procurement be collected before bids are opened?

options.text: Because declarations are accepted by the commercial team only before the closing date
So conflicts can be handled before anyone sees any bid, which protects the evaluation
Because bidders have a right to read them before they submit their tenders
Because early declarations make written evaluation criteria unnecessary

questions.hint: Prior declaration protects the integrity of scoring.

questions.prompt: An evaluator expects to be offered a job by one of the bidders. What is the right approach?

options.text: Score that bidder slightly lower than others to compensate for the interest
Say nothing until the job offer is made and then decide what to do
Declare it and step back from evaluating that bid
Evaluate as normal but ask a colleague to review the score afterwards

questions.hint: Prospective employment is a conflict that should be declared.

questions.prompt: A conflict has been declared on a project. Which statement about the response is correct?

options.text: Stepping back from the affected decision is usually safest, though the person need not always leave the whole project
Every declared conflict means the person must leave the department altogether
Once a conflict has been declared, it is treated as removed from that point on
The requirement to step back applies only to people at Grade 7 and above

questions.hint: The remedy is proportionate to the link.

questions.prompt: Why keep a written record of a declaration and of how it was handled?

options.text: It is needed so that the person's pay can be adjusted to reflect the conflict
It must be sent to every bidder so that they can comment on it
It shows a fair process and protects those involved from later challenge
It lets the register be amended later if the conflict seems less serious

questions.hint: Records support accountability.

questions.prompt: Someone took part in scoring a bid and a conflict, undeclared, later comes to light. What is a likely consequence?

options.text: The process may be challenged or the contract decision reviewed
Nothing follows, provided the winning bid was in fact the best one
The conflict is treated as cancelled because the outcome was fair
The ICO automatically takes over the decision on the contract

questions.hint: Undeclared conflicts can unwind decisions.

questions.prompt: A manager knows a candidate only through occasional professional contact. What is the position?

options.text: It is always a conflict, so the manager must leave the panel
It is not automatically a conflict, though any closer relationship should be declared
It is irrelevant, however close the relationship may become
It need be disclosed to the candidate only, not to the panel chair

questions.hint: Acquaintance is not automatically a conflict.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical source of a procurement conflict?

options.text: A shared train commute with a bidder's representative
A press release issued by a bidder during the process
A reference to a bidder in a published report
A shareholding in one of the bidding companies

questions.hint: Financial interest is a classic conflict.

items.title: L12: Gifts, hospitality and events in practice
items.source: Civil Service Code; departmental gifts and hospitality policies, GOV.UK
items.body: Day-to-day questions about gifts and hospitality rarely arrive in a clean form. A supplier offers tickets to a conference, with lunch included. A stakeholder invites a team to a reception. A grateful member of the public sends a box of biscuits. A long-standing partner offers a seat at a sporting or cultural event. The Civil Service Code principle is that you should not accept anything that might reasonably be seen to compromise your judgement or integrity. Departmental policies add detail, usually through a combination of a register, an approval route and guidance on typical values. Several factors help to judge an offer. One is the relationship of the giver to the department: a supplier in a live tender, or a body that is regulated or funded by your department, creates higher risk. Another is the value and nature of the offer: a sandwich lunch at a working meeting is different from a luxury weekend. A third is the purpose: attending to learn or to represent the department can be legitimate, while pure entertainment is more difficult to justify. A fourth is who pays: sometimes the department should pay its own way, for example for travel and accommodation. A fifth is transparency: could you comfortably explain it publicly? Gifts to the team, such as biscuits, are often shared and recorded rather than refused, although practice varies. Offers addressed to you personally, rather than the department, deserve extra care. If you are unsure, ask before you accept, not afterwards. Where you must decline, do so politely and explain that rules prevent acceptance, which usually maintains the relationship.

questions.prompt: A supplier in a live tender offers you a conference ticket with lunch included. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept the ticket but pay for the lunch yourself, to keep the offer modest
Decline and record the offer, since the supplier has a live commercial interest
Accept, since conferences are professional events with a learning purpose
Accept if the supplier confirms in writing that the offer is unconnected to the tender

questions.hint: A live tender raises the risk whatever the offer.

questions.prompt: Which factor most increases the risk of accepting an offer?

options.text: The giver being a charity with a good reputation
The giver having a long history of working with the department
The giver being regulated or funded by your department
The offer being made in person rather than by email

questions.hint: Dependent relationships raise concerns.

questions.prompt: A box of biscuits arrives from a grateful member of the public. What do departments commonly do?

options.text: Share them with the team and record the gift if policy requires it
Return them by post with a formal letter of refusal
Allow the recipient to keep them as a personal gift
Refuse them in every case, whatever the value

questions.hint: Small gifts are often shared and recorded.

questions.prompt: Which offer is hardest to justify under the Code?

options.text: A working lunch at a meeting called to discuss the contract with the supplier concerned
A seat at an event where you are attending in order to represent the department
Light refreshments at a briefing run by a partner organisation for several departments
A day of pure entertainment from a company with whom you do business

questions.hint: Pure entertainment from a commercial partner is hard to defend.

questions.prompt: When might a department pay its own way for an event it attends?

options.text: Only when the cost exceeds an amount the giver has set
Never, because offers should always be accepted if made in good faith
Only when the event is held outside the United Kingdom
For costs such as travel and accommodation, where acceptance could compromise independence

questions.hint: Paying its own way preserves independence.

questions.prompt: Why does an offer addressed to you personally deserve extra care?

options.text: Personal offers must always be declined without discussion
Personal offers do not need to be recorded in the register
It may suggest the giver is trying to influence you rather than the department
Personal offers may be accepted without any approval

questions.hint: Personal targeting can imply influence.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to ask whether you may accept an offer you are unsure about?

options.text: Before you accept it
After you have attended the event, so you know what it involved
Only if someone later complains about it
At your next performance appraisal

questions.hint: Ask first, not afterwards.

questions.prompt: How should a manager decline a gift while keeping a good working relationship?

options.text: Leave it unopened and say nothing about it
Thank the giver and explain that the rules prevent acceptance
Say that it does not meet the department's standard of value
Pass it quietly to a colleague who is not covered by the rules

questions.hint: Politeness preserves the relationship.

questions.prompt: Which question best helps you judge an offer?

options.text: Could I comfortably explain accepting it in public?
Would the giver be offended and feel the relationship harmed if I declined the offer?
Do other colleagues in my team also accept offers of this kind from time to time?
Is it cheaper than the equivalent offer that the same organisation made last year?

questions.hint: Transparency is a good test.

questions.prompt: An event invitation addressed to the whole team comes from a stakeholder. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Accept for everyone without checking, as the invitation was to the team
Decline for everyone without considering the purpose of the event
Let each person decide privately, with no record kept
Check policy, seek approval and record attendance, judging the purpose and the cost

questions.hint: Team offers still need approval.

items.title: L12: Outside interests, social media and politics at senior-ish grades
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code; Social media guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: As you move from EO to HEO and SEO, your public profile can matter more, because people see you as a representative of a team or policy area. The Civil Service Code requires impartiality: you should carry out your role with dedication and a commitment to the Civil Service and its core values, and serve the government of the day whatever its political persuasion. That affects what you say and do outside work. Outside interests such as company directorships, paid consultancy, trusteeships, school governorships or elected local office should be declared, and in many cases need permission. They should not conflict with your duties, use official time or information, or create a risk to the reputation of the department. Questions of political activity are governed by the Civil Service Management Code's categories of politically free, intermediate and politically restricted posts. Many posts at HEO and SEO level are likely to be in an intermediate group, though the exact classification depends on the department and the role, and the Senior Civil Service is politically restricted. Do not assume which category applies: check. Social media adds particular risks. Even a personal account can be read as a view of the civil service if your role is identifiable. Avoid expressing partisan views, criticising ministers or policy in your area, or sharing material that could embarrass the department. The 'public square' test is a good one: if you would not say it in a public meeting with your name and job title on display, do not post it. Privacy settings do not remove the duty, and deleting a post does not undo the harm. Remember that your obligations about confidential material continue on social media as elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why does a growing public profile matter as someone moves from EO towards SEO?

options.text: Higher grades are legally banned from speaking in public about any aspect of their work
Others may read what they say as representing their team or policy area
Higher grades lose the right to hold any outside interest while they remain in post
Higher grades are always classified as politically free, so they can say what they like

questions.hint: Perceived representation increases the importance of impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which outside interest is most likely to need declaration and permission?

options.text: A subscription to a monthly book club run by an outside group of friends
A membership of a local gym that the person attends before the working day begins
A paid directorship of a private company
Voting in a local election and attending the count as a member of the public

questions.hint: Directorships can conflict with duties.

questions.prompt: What is the right approach to finding out which political activity category applies to your post?

options.text: Assume the category matches your grade in every department
Assume all HEO posts are politically free
Ask a colleague with the same job title in another department
Check, because the classification depends on the department and the role

questions.hint: Do not assume.

questions.prompt: What is the 'public square' test for a social media post?

options.text: Would it be popular with the people who follow you?
Would you say it in a public meeting with your name and job title on display?
Would it be acceptable if posted from an anonymous account?
Would your colleagues find it amusing?

questions.hint: Identifiable civil servants are held to a public standard.

questions.prompt: A civil servant deletes a social media post that breached the guidance. What is the position?

options.text: The harm may already be done, because the post may have been seen or copied
Deletion removes every record of it, so the breach is treated as undone
Deletion within a day of posting returns things to how they were before
Deletion counts as a remedy once the account has been set to private

questions.hint: Deleting does not erase the effect.

questions.prompt: A civil servant uses a private account but names their department in the bio. How might their posts be read?

options.text: As entirely private, because the account is personal
As protected by the Equality Act in every case
As reflecting on the department, even if described as personal views
As approved by the department's press office

questions.hint: An identifiable role means posts can be read as official.

questions.prompt: Which post is most likely to breach the duty of impartiality?

options.text: A photo of a family holiday
A report of a charity run you completed
A thank-you to your team after a successful event
A partisan comment attacking a minister on your own policy area

questions.hint: Partisan comment on your own policy area is risky.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to stand as a local councillor. What should they do first?

options.text: Stand first and tell the department afterwards
Assume local office is allowed for everyone
Ask the line manager or propriety team about the rules and permission required
Ask the party to confirm whether the civil service rules matter

questions.hint: Seek permission before taking steps.

questions.prompt: Which statement about privacy settings on social media is right?

options.text: They do not remove the duty of impartiality and confidentiality
They make it safe to express any view among friends
They apply only to the Senior Civil Service
They exempt posts from the Civil Service Code

questions.hint: Private does not mean unaccountable.

questions.prompt: Which outside role is most likely to conflict with official duties?

options.text: A trusteeship of a charity unconnected to your work
A trusteeship of a charity that receives grants from your department
A volunteer role at a youth club
A parent-teacher association role at your child's school

questions.hint: Links to funded bodies create conflicts.

items.title: L12: Official secrets, publication and approaches
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; National Security Act 2023, legislation.gov.uk
items.body: The confidentiality duty is tested in practice when civil servants want to speak, write or publish, or when someone approaches them. A civil servant who is asked to speak at a conference about their work should seek approval and clarify what may be said, because even apparently general remarks about current work can reveal sensitive information. A civil servant who writes a book, article or blog about government work, whether current or after leaving, should check whether it relies on official information and, if so, follow the department's procedures for clearance before publication. The Official Secrets Act 1989 applies to former staff as well as serving ones, and unauthorised disclosure of information in the protected categories can be a criminal offence. For some categories, the offence depends on proof that damage was caused, and for others, such as security and intelligence material held by those in those services, it does not. There is no general public interest defence in that Act, which is why internal routes and the Code's procedures matter. A person who has concerns should use the proper channels. Approaches are another risk. Foreign intelligence services and other hostile actors sometimes use friendly contacts, online networking, job offers, consultancy requests or hospitality to gain information over time. The National Security Act 2023 criminalises assisting a foreign intelligence service and certain forms of foreign interference. A good test is to ask whether the contact is asking for information that is not public, whether it is offering something unusual in return, and whether the relationship is growing too fast. Report anything that seems odd, even if you are unsure. The security team would rather receive ten harmless reports than miss one that matters.

questions.prompt: A civil servant is invited to speak at a conference about their current work. What should they do first?

options.text: Accept, then decide what to include once they see the audience on the day
Accept, but avoid naming the department so that nothing is attributed
Decline all public speaking, since any talk about current work is forbidden
Seek approval and clarify what may be said before agreeing to speak

questions.hint: Approval before speaking protects both the person and the information.

questions.prompt: A civil servant plans a book drawing on their government career, to be published after they retire. What should they do?

options.text: Publish when ready, because the rules stop applying once employment has ended
Change the names of the people involved and publish without further checks
Check whether it relies on official information and follow the department's clearance procedure
Publish only material that has appeared in newspapers, without asking anyone

questions.hint: The duty continues after leaving, and clearance procedures apply.

questions.prompt: Does the Official Secrets Act 1989 apply to former civil servants?

options.text: It ends when their employment ends, along with their contract
It continues to apply to them after they leave the service
It applies only if they move to another government post
It applies only to former staff who held Developed Vetting

questions.hint: The duty is lifelong.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Official Secrets Act 1989 is accurate?

options.text: It contains no general public interest defence, which is why proper internal routes matter
It contains a broad public interest defence covering any disclosure of wrongdoing
It covers only information that carries a formal security classification marking
It applies only to disclosures made to national newspapers

questions.hint: Without a general defence, raising concerns properly is the safe path.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is most likely to suggest a hostile approach?

options.text: A colleague from another department asks how your project is going over coffee
A press officer sends you a press release about a published announcement
A conference organiser confirms your booking and the session timings
A new online contact asks for non-public information and offers something unusual in return

questions.hint: Non-public requests plus unusual rewards are warning signs.

questions.prompt: Which of these could a hostile actor use to gather information gradually?

options.text: Friendly networking, consultancy offers and hospitality that build a relationship
Published statistics and annual reports that are freely available to anyone
Open parliamentary debates reported in the public record
Press releases issued by the department's communications team

questions.hint: Hostile actors build relationships over time.

questions.prompt: Which of these is conduct the National Security Act 2023 addresses?

options.text: Taking annual leave without telling a line manager in advance
Assisting a foreign intelligence service in its work against the United Kingdom
Using social media for personal views outside working hours
Making personal phone calls from the workplace

questions.hint: The Act is aimed at state threats.

questions.prompt: A civil servant is unsure whether a new contact is a security risk. What is the best course?

options.text: Wait until the contact asks for something clearly improper before acting
Confront the contact and ask directly what they want
Report it to security even if unsure, and let them assess it
Say nothing, to avoid raising a false alarm over an innocent person

questions.hint: Early reporting lets specialists assess.

questions.prompt: Why would security teams rather receive several harmless reports than miss one real one?

options.text: Reports are counted towards each security team's annual performance targets and funding
Harmless reports cancel out serious ones in the monthly figures
Early reports let them spot patterns and act before harm is done
Each report earns the reporting officer a recognition payment

questions.hint: Early reporting protects the department.

questions.prompt: Which feature suggests a relationship with a new contact is developing too quickly?

options.text: Frequent requests for information that is not public, with rising offers in return
A shared interest in a hobby that you have mentioned online
Regular, polite emails about arrangements for an agreed meeting
A reference to people you both know in the same profession

questions.hint: Speed and non-public requests are warning signs.

items.title: L12: Raising concerns in difficult circumstances
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Raising a concern is easy when the route is clear and the person at the other end is trusted. It is harder when your line manager is the person you are concerned about, when the problem is shared by your team, or when you fear you may be wrong. The Civil Service Code says you should report the matter in accordance with the relevant procedures, usually to your line manager or someone in your management chain. If the line manager is involved you can go to a more senior manager, a nominated officer, a confidential helpline, HR or the propriety and ethics team. The Civil Service Commission is the independent route if you have raised a concern and are not satisfied, or if you are asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code. A concern can be about illegal acts, improper behaviour, waste, safety, a breach of the Code, or an instruction to act against its values. You do not need proof; you need to have a reasonable belief and to give the facts you know. It helps to write down what you saw, when, and who else knew, and to stick to what you can say rather than guess. If a manager receives a concern, they should record it, avoid promising absolute secrecy that they may not be able to give, protect the person from any form of retaliation, and pass it on appropriately. Retaliation, such as unfair treatment, exclusion or a poor appraisal that follows a report, is itself serious. Many whistleblowing cases do not fail because the concern was wrong but because the person who raised it was not heard or was treated badly afterwards.

questions.prompt: Your line manager is the person you are concerned about. Where might you go?

options.text: Directly to a journalist, since the internal route is blocked by your manager
Nowhere, because the Code says you must raise it with your line manager first
To colleagues in the team, so they can agree what should be done
A more senior manager, a nominated officer, a confidential helpline or the propriety team

questions.hint: Alternative internal routes exist.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Commission offer in this context?

options.text: A service that takes over any disciplinary case from the department
An independent route if internal routes have failed or you are asked to act against the Code
A way of obtaining compensation for any complaint about a manager
A body that investigates every concern before the department does

questions.hint: The Commission is independent of departments.

questions.prompt: What standard of evidence is needed before you raise a concern under the Code?

options.text: A reasonable belief and the facts you know are enough to raise it
Documentary evidence of a kind that would stand up in court
Proof of financial loss, since concerns with no money element are not covered
Support from at least one other witness who saw the same thing

questions.hint: Reasonable belief is the standard.

questions.prompt: What is it sensible to record when you raise a concern?

options.text: Your opinion of the person's character and how they treat others
Your guess about the person's motive and likely next step
What you saw, when it happened and who else may have known
A list of rumours colleagues have shared about the same person

questions.hint: Stick to facts you can state.

questions.prompt: A manager receives a concern from a team member. Which action would be a mistake?

options.text: Writing down accurately what was said and the date on which it was said to them
Promising absolute secrecy that they may not be able to keep
Passing the concern on to the right place so that it can be examined properly
Making sure the person is protected from any retaliation or unfair treatment after reporting

questions.hint: Do not over-promise confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest example of retaliation after a concern has been raised?

options.text: An invitation to the routine monthly team meeting that the whole team attends
A message thanking the person for raising the concern and acknowledging the effort
A note telling the person clearly what will happen next and when to expect it
A poor appraisal that follows the report without any good reason

questions.hint: Unfair treatment as a result is detriment.

questions.prompt: Why do many whistleblowing cases go badly?

options.text: Often because the person was not listened to, or was treated badly after speaking up
Because concerns raised by civil servants are almost always wrong
Because the Civil Service Code forbids staff from raising any concern
Because the Commission rejects most concerns it receives

questions.hint: Handling after the report matters greatly.

questions.prompt: Which situation falls within the Code's procedures for raising concerns?

options.text: A disagreement about which team should be given the desks nearest the window
Being told to act in a way that conflicts with the Code's values
A preference for a different name for the team, which the manager has declined
A dislike of the department's choice of canteen supplier after a change of contract

questions.hint: Instructions that conflict with the Code count.

questions.prompt: A staff member raises a concern about a senior colleague. What should the manager avoid?

options.text: Writing down accurately what was said by the person and when it was said
Referring the matter to the right body so that it can be properly examined
Telling the senior colleague who raised it, without need or agreement
Making sure that the person is protected from any detriment

questions.hint: Confidentiality protects the person raising the concern.

questions.prompt: A civil servant fears they may be wrong about a concern. What is the sound approach?

options.text: Wait until they are completely certain, however long that takes, before saying anything
Investigate privately for several months before telling anyone
Ask colleagues to vote on whether the concern is serious enough
Raise it with the facts they know, since reasonable belief is enough

questions.hint: Specialists test the concern; the person need not prove it.

items.title: L12: Probation in practice
items.source: Departmental probation policies; Civil Service Management Code; Equality Act 2010, GOV.UK
items.body: A manager's duty on probation is to make the process fair, evidence-based and supportive. Probation policies vary between departments and contracts, so you should always check your own, but several principles are common. Objectives should be clear and agreed early. Feedback should be regular, specific and recorded. Concerns should be raised as soon as they appear, not stored until the end. Where performance falls short, the manager should explain what is expected, offer support, and give a fair chance to improve. Where the person has a disability, reasonable adjustments must be considered and made, and the Equality Act applies from the first day. Absence during probation, for example sickness or parental leave, is usually handled by adjusting or extending the review timeline in line with policy, not by treating the absence itself as poor performance. If the person is pregnant, on maternity leave or has a protected characteristic, extra care is needed to ensure that any decision is not influenced by it. Probation can result in confirmation in post, an extension where there is a reasonable prospect of improvement, or, in serious cases, a dismissal or an end of the appointment. Whatever the outcome, the manager should give the decision in time, put it in writing and explain the reasons. A common failure is a manager who avoids a difficult conversation for months and then recommends failure at the last moment without any earlier warning. Another is passing someone who is not yet meeting the standard because it is easier than dealing with the problem. Both are unfair, to the person and to the department. Keep the HR team informed so that process and law are followed.

questions.prompt: A probationer has not met an objective after six weeks. What is the best response?

options.text: Wait until the end of probation, so the whole period can be judged together
Mention it to the team informally, so everyone can help the person improve
Move the person to a different project without telling them why
Discuss it, explain the standard, offer support and record the conversation

questions.hint: Early, supported feedback is fairest.

questions.prompt: How is absence during probation, such as sickness or parental leave, usually treated?

options.text: As evidence of poor performance when the final decision is made
By adjusting or extending the review timetable in line with policy
As a reason to end probation early without a review
As irrelevant, so that the original timetable still applies in full

questions.hint: Absence should not count against the person.

questions.prompt: When do reasonable adjustments for a disabled probationer need to be considered?

options.text: From the first day, because the Equality Act applies throughout
Only after probation has been passed and the person is confirmed
Only if the person puts the request in writing within a month
Only for those on permanent rather than fixed-term contracts

questions.hint: The Act applies from day one.

questions.prompt: Which outcome may suit a probationer with a reasonable prospect of improving?

options.text: Automatic dismissal at the end of the standard period
A transfer to another department without a review
An extension of probation with clear objectives and support
Early confirmation in post, to boost the person's confidence

questions.hint: Extensions can be used where improvement is likely.

questions.prompt: What is a common failure in probation management?

options.text: Avoiding a difficult conversation, then recommending failure at the end with no earlier warning
Holding regular one-to-ones and recording the main points of each
Agreeing objectives with the person in the first few weeks
Telling HR about concerns as soon as they become serious

questions.hint: Late surprise is unfair to the person.

questions.prompt: Why is it a poor choice to confirm someone who is not yet meeting the standard?

options.text: It is unlawful for a manager to confirm anyone while any concerns remain outstanding
It means the manager takes over responsibility for the person's work
It is unfair to the person and to the department, and it stores up the problem
It voids the person's contract and requires a new appointment

questions.hint: Honest assessment is part of the duty.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a probation decision?

options.text: A verbal comment in passing, to keep the tone informal
A message to the whole team, so that everyone knows the outcome
A summary of the person's pay and expected progression
Written confirmation and clear reasons, given in good time

questions.hint: Decisions should be clear and timely.

questions.prompt: Why involve HR in a probation case where there are concerns?

options.text: To let HR decide the outcome in place of the manager
To make sure that the department's process and the law are followed
To avoid the need to keep any written record at all
To allow the manager to stay out of the conversation with the person

questions.hint: HR supports fair process.

questions.prompt: A pregnant probationer is struggling with an objective. What extra care is needed?

options.text: Make sure any decision is not influenced by the pregnancy and that the law is followed
Ignore the pregnancy altogether and treat the person exactly like any other
End probation early, so the issue is settled before leave begins
Suggest quietly that the person resigns before the issue is raised formally

questions.hint: Protected characteristics require care.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest kind of evidence in a probation record?

options.text: The manager's general impression of the person's attitude and enthusiasm in the role
Dated, specific examples of work measured against the agreed objectives
Comments from colleagues about the person's life outside work
A single summary written in the final week, drawing on what the manager remembers

questions.hint: Specific, dated evidence is strongest.

items.title: L12: Recruitment checks in practice
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Recruitment Principles, GOV.UK
items.body: Checks look simple on a form but raise practical questions. Consider gaps in employment history. The baseline standard asks for a record of the recent past, usually three years, with any gaps accounted for. A gap is not a problem in itself; candidates may have been studying, caring, travelling or unwell. The question is whether the gap has been explained honestly. If a reference or record does not match what the candidate said, the first step is to ask neutrally. Dates may differ because of a clerical error, a change of company name or a mistaken memory. A mismatch that cannot be explained, or a false statement, may lead to the offer being withdrawn, and HR will guide the decision. Candidates with unspent convictions must declare them in the way set by the form. The conviction is considered in relation to the role, and a declared one is not necessarily a barrier. Those who work through agencies or as contractors are also expected to meet equivalent checks before they get access to government systems or premises. If a person is returning to the Civil Service, you cannot assume that earlier checks are still valid. The department decides whether existing clearance or checks can be relied on and whether they must be redone. Use the same standard for every candidate, and avoid informal shortcuts for people who seem trustworthy or are well recommended. Candidates are entitled to fair treatment and to know what is required. Keep personal data to those who need it, and do not discuss one candidate's check results with other staff or candidates. Delays are common, so keep the candidate informed and avoid giving access in advance.

questions.prompt: A candidate has a nine-month gap in their recent history. What is the correct view?

options.text: The gap automatically disqualifies the candidate from the role, whatever the explanation given
The gap may be ignored if the rest of the employment history is complete and consistent
The gap must be treated in the same way as an unspent conviction
A gap is not a problem in itself, but it should be explained honestly

questions.hint: Honest explanation is the issue.

questions.prompt: A reference gives different dates from those on the candidate's form. What is the right first step?

options.text: Withdraw the offer immediately, since a mismatch shows dishonesty
Ignore it, because small differences are always clerical mistakes
Ask the candidate neutrally, as it may be an error or a change of company name
Ask the candidate's colleagues which dates are right

questions.hint: Check before assuming dishonesty.

questions.prompt: What may follow an unexplained false statement on a form?

options.text: The candidate is asked to start with a longer probation period
The offer may be withdrawn, following guidance from HR
The candidate is moved to a lower grade
The statement is noted and no action is taken

questions.hint: False statements are serious.

questions.prompt: How is a declared unspent conviction usually treated?

options.text: It always rules the candidate out of every Civil Service post
It is ignored if the candidate has since worked elsewhere
It is considered in relation to the role and is not necessarily a barrier
It is shared with the rest of the team for a view

questions.hint: Relevance to the role matters.

questions.prompt: An agency worker will use government systems. What is the general position on checks?

options.text: They are expected to meet equivalent checks before they are given access
None are needed, because the agency is their employer and has checked them
A single reference from the agency is all that is required
Checks apply only to permanent civil servants, not to temporary workers

questions.hint: Equivalent checks apply to those with access.

questions.prompt: A former civil servant is returning to the department. What should the manager assume about earlier checks?

options.text: That they remain valid for life, whatever has changed since
That they have expired automatically and everything must be repeated
That they no longer matter, since the person has served before
That the department will decide whether they can be relied on or must be redone

questions.hint: Do not assume validity either way.

questions.prompt: Which practice in checking is poor?

options.text: Using the same standard for every candidate for the same role
Telling candidates clearly what is needed and by when
Keeping the candidate informed when checks are delayed
Skipping checks for a well-recommended candidate, because they seem trustworthy

questions.hint: Informal shortcuts undermine fairness.

questions.prompt: Why should one candidate's check results not be discussed with other staff?

options.text: The information is personal data and should go only to those who need it
The results are public records that anyone can ask for
Candidates must compete against each other on the results of their checks, so these are shared
Open discussion helps the team to decide more fairly

questions.hint: Data protection and fairness apply.

questions.prompt: Checks are delayed but the team is busy. What should the manager do?

options.text: Give access, since the delay is not the candidate's fault
Cancel the offer, so that a faster candidate can be found to fill the vacancy quickly
Keep the candidate informed and avoid giving access in advance
